_note: Original text written for INTUITY to the Cambridge B2 First Part 5 specification (about 600 words, six questions in text order). Test 5 mixes the question types: attitude, inference, reference ('it'), purpose ('Why does the writer mention…?'), the meaning of a phrase, and a final question that links the ending back to the opening. Each card is a chunk of the article with the question it answers; `highlight` is the sentence that proves the answer, `why` explains the distractors. Used by the Part 5 practice page and by Full test 5.
title: Night shift
subtitle: Camera operator Maisie Hale, 24, spent seven months filming a single hedgehog in a suburban back garden. She explains why it was the best job she has ever had.

cards.text: When Maisie Hale was offered the job, she very nearly turned it down. At twenty-four, she had already spent two years as an assistant on nature programmes, carrying tripods up Scottish hillsides and waiting on freezing beaches for seals that rarely appeared. She had been hoping, she admits, for something more exotic: snow leopards, perhaps, or whales. Instead the producer wanted seven months of night filming in a back garden in Norwich, following one hedgehog. 'I thought it was a joke,' she says. 'Then I thought it was a punishment. It took me about a day to realise it was the chance I'd been waiting for.'
cards.question: How did Maisie feel when she was first offered the job?
choices: She was worried that she did not have enough experience.
She was annoyed that it meant leaving Scotland.
She was excited to be working on her own at last.
She was disappointed that it was not more adventurous.
cards.highlight: She had been hoping, she admits, for something more exotic: snow leopards, perhaps, or whales.
cards.why: She wanted 'something more exotic' and at first saw a garden hedgehog as 'a punishment'. Her two years as an assistant are mentioned, but she never doubts her experience; the excitement came only a day later.

cards.text: The hedgehog, a young female the crew named Bramble, had been chosen because she visited the same garden almost every night. Its owners, a retired couple called the Pikes, had been leaving out food and water for her for a year, and they agreed to let a film crew of one take over their shed. Maisie set up four small infrared cameras, which the animal could not see, and spent the first fortnight simply watching the screens without recording anything. 'Everyone told me I was wasting time,' she says. 'But I didn't know her yet. If I'd started filming straight away, I'd have been filming in the wrong places.'
cards.question: What can we infer about Maisie's first two weeks in the garden?
choices: She believed she had to learn Bramble's habits before she could film her well.
She could not record anything because the cameras were not ready.
She was waiting for the Pikes to agree to let her use the shed.
She later accepted that the time had been wasted.
cards.highlight: If I'd started filming straight away, I'd have been filming in the wrong places.
cards.why: 'I didn't know her yet': watching first showed her where to point the cameras. The cameras were already set up, and 'Everyone told me I was wasting time' is other people's view, which she rejects.

cards.text: Hedgehogs, Maisie quickly discovered, are not the slow, sleepy creatures of children's books. Bramble regularly travelled more than two kilometres in a night, squeezing under fences and through gaps in hedges, and she would often disappear from the garden for hours. Following her meant borrowing a second set of cameras and asking permission from a dozen neighbours, most of whom were delighted to help. One elderly man even cut a small hole at the bottom of his garden gate. 'He said he'd always wanted to do it anyway,' Maisie laughs, 'and Bramble used it the very next night.'
cards.question: What does 'it' refer to in 'Bramble used it the very next night'?
choices: the garden belonging to the Pikes
a gap in one of the neighbours' hedges
the opening the elderly man made
the second set of cameras
cards.highlight: One elderly man even cut a small hole at the bottom of his garden gate.
cards.why: 'It' is the 'small hole at the bottom of his garden gate', which Bramble went through the following night. Gaps in hedges are mentioned earlier, but as something she used already, not something new.

cards.text: The work was lonely and oddly timed. Maisie slept from nine in the morning until four in the afternoon, ate breakfast at teatime, saw almost nothing of her friends for months, and spent most nights in the Pikes' shed wrapped in two sleeping bags. Mrs Pike brought her a flask of soup at midnight without fail, and on one occasion a hot-water bottle in a knitted cover shaped like a hedgehog. Maisie still has it. 'I was there to look after Bramble,' she says, 'but really the Pikes were looking after both of us.'
cards.question: Why does the writer mention the hot-water bottle?
choices: to suggest that Mrs Pike did not take the filming seriously
to show the care Maisie received from the people whose garden she used
to give an example of how Maisie kept herself awake at night
to show how interested the Pikes had become in hedgehogs
cards.highlight: but really the Pikes were looking after both of us
cards.why: The soup 'without fail' and the hot-water bottle lead to 'the Pikes were looking after both of us'. The hedgehog cover is a joke, not evidence that Mrs Pike thought the work silly or was now fascinated by hedgehogs.

cards.text: The moment Maisie is proudest of came in late spring, when Bramble gave birth to four hoglets somewhere under the Pikes' shed. For three weeks the mother barely appeared, and Maisie began to fear that something had gone wrong. Then, one warm night in June, Bramble led her family out across the lawn in a wobbly line. Maisie had exactly one camera in the right place. 'I'd moved it there that afternoon on a hunch,' she says. 'If I'd left it where it was, I'd have got a beautiful shot of an empty flowerbed.'
cards.question: What does Maisie mean when she says she moved the camera 'on a hunch'?
choices: She was following a plan she had made several weeks earlier.
She had been told by the Pikes that the hoglets were about to appear.
She wanted to keep the camera away from the flowerbed.
She acted on a feeling rather than on any clear evidence.
cards.highlight: I'd moved it there that afternoon on a hunch
cards.why: A hunch is a guess based on feeling: she moved it 'that afternoon', and only luck stopped her filming 'an empty flowerbed'. For three weeks she had no evidence at all, so it was not a plan, and the Pikes are not mentioned.

cards.text: The finished film lasts fifty-two minutes and will be shown on television next spring. Maisie has since been offered work abroad, including a month filming whales off the coast of Norway, and she has accepted. But she admits that the offer did not excite her quite as much as she had expected. Bramble still visits the Pikes' garden most nights, without a film crew now, and Mrs Pike sends regular updates. 'People ask whether I'll miss filming something so small,' Maisie says. 'Honestly? I think the whales are going to have to work quite hard to impress me.'
cards.question: What does the final paragraph suggest about Maisie?
choices: She regrets accepting the job in Norway.
Her time with Bramble has changed what she values in her work.
She intends to go back and film Bramble again.
She is worried that the film will not be popular.
cards.highlight: I think the whales are going to have to work quite hard to impress me.
cards.why: In the first paragraph she longed for whales; now 'the whales are going to have to work quite hard to impress me'. She is less excited than expected, but nothing suggests she regrets accepting, and Mrs Pike's updates are not a plan to return.
